Data governance in public health refers to the organised system that guides how health data is handled from the moment it is collected to the moment it is archived. It defines who is responsible for data, who is allowed to access it, and what standards must be followed to protect it. This framework is essential in public health because it ensures that data is used ethically and legally, while creating conditions for high-quality analysis and effective collaboration. [1]

It helps ensure that data is used responsibly, with clear roles, access, and safeguards in place to protect sensitive personal information. This framework rests on five core principles: data stewardship and ownership, controlled access and responsible sharing, privacy, confidentiality, and security. [2][3]

The key dimensions of data quality are Accuracy, Completeness, Timeliness, and Validity. [1][2]

A typical 4-step quality assurance process for public health data starts with basic validation at the point of data entry, followed by supervisors or information officers reviewing reports, comparing them with previous periods, and following up on unusual values or missing submissions. At intervals, teams may verify figures against source documents, such as clinic registers, and correct errors where needed. Feedback to facilities closes the loop, explaining what went wrong and helping prevent the same problems in future. Some programmes also organise more formal data quality audits, where selected indicators are systematically checked across several sites to identify common weaknesses. [2]

When interpreting a public health time series, the key features to look for are: Level - the overall height of the series, indicating whether the indicator is at a low, moderate, or high level; Trend - the long-term direction, indicating whether there is a gradual increase, decrease, or stable pattern over months or years; Seasonality - repeating patterns, indicating whether values rise and fall in a regular cycle; and Unusual peaks or drops - deviations from the usual pattern, indicating sudden spikes or sharp drops that may signal an outbreak or other issues [1].

Generalised Linear Models (GLMs) are statistical models that quantify which factors drive patterns, clarify relationships between risk factors and outcomes, and estimate the association between characteristics and key health events. They are useful in public health as they help identify who is most at risk and predict important outcomes in a transparent and interpretable way [1][2]. GLMs can handle different types of data, including binary outcomes, and are the logical next step to make analysis more sophisticated [2]. They provide a foundation for machine learning and text analytics methods that follow.

Logistic regression is used for binary outcomes, predicting whether an event (e.g. getting sick) is likely to happen [1][3]. Poisson regression is used for count outcomes, predicting how often events (e.g. disease cases) occur over time or across places [1][3]. The main difference between the two is the type of outcome they model, with logistic regression handling binary outcomes and Poisson regression handling count outcomes [1][3]. This distinction is crucial in public health decision-making, as it enables professionals to estimate risks, counts, and rates accurately [1].
GLMs can handle binary outcomes, count data, and continuous data. [2] [2][3]

Machine Learning differs from traditional statistical models in public health because it learns complex patterns from data to make predictions, whereas traditional models explain relationships and estimate risks using interpretable statistical models. [2][3] Machine Learning is particularly useful for forecasting outcomes, flagging high-risk cases, and supporting decisions in situations where traditional models may struggle. [2] It complements traditional statistical methods by providing a more nuanced understanding of public health data. [2]

In supervised learning, features are inputs or characteristics of a case, and labels are the corresponding known outcomes or classifications. [1] Features are the variables or attributes used to describe a case, while labels are the actual outcomes or classifications assigned to those cases. [1]

A random forest combines the predictions of its trees by taking a majority vote across the trees for categorical outcomes and calculating an average for numerical outcomes. This aggregation cancels out individual quirks and produces a more stable, reliable prediction. [1][2]

A model can easily look "excellent" on the same data it was trained on, simply because it has memorised many details instead of identifying learning patterns, this phenomenon is called overfitting [1][2]. To avoid it, analysts usually split the data into a training set and a test set, and then check the model on the test set to see how well it is likely to perform on data it has never seen before [2]. This shows how well it is likely to perform on new patients, facilities, or districts, and helps to identify practical issues such as under-representation of certain groups in the training data [2]. This can lead to systematically biased predictions for these groups [2].
